**Surat al-Kafirun**

It is also called al-Muqashqisha, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zurara ibn Awfa. The word derives from *qashqasha al-maridu*, meaning the sick person recovered and was healed, that is, the surah frees its reciter from shirk and hypocrisy. It is also called, as in *Jamal al-Qurra'*, Surat al-'Ibadah (the Surah of Worship), and likewise Surat al-Ikhlas (the Surah of Sincerity). According to Ibn 'Abbas and the majority, it is Makki. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn al-Zubayr that it is Madani, and al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) relates this from Qatada, contrary to what is in *Majma' al-Bayan*, where he is said to hold that it is Makki. Whatever the case, the statement of al-Dawani that it is Makki by consensus is not well placed.

Its verses number six, without any disagreement. It contains a declaration of what was understood from the preceding surah concerning the command to devote worship sincerely to Him, Mighty and Majestic, and this suffices as the connection between the two.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jabala ibn Haritha, who was the brother of Zayd ibn Haritha, and who had said to him, peace be upon him: "Teach me something that I may recite when I go to sleep," and similar to that, as in a hadith reported by Imam Ahmad and al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*. He (ﷺ) also commanded Anas to recite it when he slept, giving as the reason what has been mentioned, as reported by al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*. And he, peace be upon him, commanded Khabbab likewise, as in a hadith reported by al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh.

Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not direct you to a word that will save you from associating partners with Allah, the Exalted? You recite: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ when you go to sleep."

al-Daylami reported from 'Abdullah ibn Jarad, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The hypocrite does not pray the Duha prayer, and does not recite: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾.'"

It is also recommended to recite it, together with ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, in the two rak'ahs of the Fajr Sunnah, which, according to most scholars, is the most excellent of the regular Sunnah prayers. Likewise it is recommended in the two rak'ahs after Maghrib. This is a proof against those among the imams who said that it is not recommended to add a surah to al-Fatiha in the Fajr Sunnah.

There occurs in a hadith reported by al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* from Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and in another reported by him in *al-Saghir* from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in the same manner, that it equals one quarter of the Qur'an.

Imam (al-Razi) explained this by saying that the Qur'an contains the command to do what is commanded and the prohibition of what is forbidden, and each of these either relates to the heart or to the limbs, so there are four categories. This surah contains the prohibition of the forbidden matters related to the heart, so it is like one quarter of the Qur'an. This has been criticized on the ground that worship is more general than the heart-based and the bodily, and that the commands and prohibitions related to it are not restricted to the commanded and forbidden matters of the heart and body; and that the aims of the Noble Qur'an are not confined to the aforementioned command and prohibition, but include other aims, such as the states of the origin (of creation) and the return (to the Hereafter). Hence it has been said: "Perhaps the closest view is that the aims of the Qur'an are tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness), the legal rulings, and the states of the Hereafter. Tawhid means devoting worship exclusively to Allah, the Exalted, and it is what the prophets, peace be upon them, called to first and foremost. Exclusivity is achieved only by negating the worship of other than Him, Exalted is He, and the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for exclusivity has two parts: negation regarding other than the one specified, and affirmation for the one specified. Thus the aims, by this consideration, become four. This surah includes abandoning the worship of other than Him, Glorified is He, and disavowing it; so by this consideration it is one quarter of the Qur'an. And because it does not explicitly contain the command to worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as it explicitly contains the abandonment of worship of other than Him, Exalted is He, it does not equal half the Qur'an." It has also been said: "The aims of the Qur'an are the attributes of Allah, Exalted is He, prophethood, the legal rulings, and admonitions, and the surah contains the foundation of the first, which is tawhid; therefore it equals one quarter of it." Some of my eminent contemporary friends mentioned several explanations for this, the best of which, in my view, is that the religion contained in the Qur'an has four types: acts of worship, transactions, crimes, and marriages. This surah contains the first type, and so it is one quarter. This has been criticized: if he meant that it is one quarter of the Qur'an, then we do not accept the validity of deriving it from the claim that the religion contained in the Qur'an has four types; and if he meant that it is one quarter of the religion, then that is not the subject under discussion, since the subject is whether it equals one quarter of the Qur'an, which is what the reports indicate through their differing wordings. The necessary connection between the two is not granted, and moreover the true opposition among the mentioned types is not complete. It has been answered by the possibility that he meant that the aims of the Qur'an are those four which constitute the religion, and it is not far-fetched that the inclusion of any one of them equals the whole Qur'an in its aims and in other matters. The restriction is not undermined by the fact that among its aims are the states of the origin and the return; for their inclusion within acts of worship in a certain sense, and the absence of true opposition, is not harmful, since it suffices for the purpose that common usage counts those matters as opposites, even if only in a conventional sense. So reflect on all of this. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Guide to the most upright paths.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾. The eminent exegetes said: the intended ones are specific disbelievers from Quraysh, of whom Allah, the Exalted, had known that faith would never come from them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* reported from Sa'id ibn Mina, client of Abu al-Bakhtari, who said: "al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and Umayya ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come, worship what we worship, and we will worship what you worship, and we will share with you in our whole affair. If what we are upon is better than what you are upon, you will have taken a share of it; and if what you are upon is better than what we are upon, we will have taken a share of it.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ until the surah ended."

In another report: "A group of the stubborn ones of Quraysh said to him (ﷺ): 'Come, follow our religion and we will follow yours. You worship our gods for one year, and we will worship your God for one year.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I seek refuge with Allah from associating anything with Allah, Glorified is He.' They said: 'Then touch some of our gods, and we will believe you and worship your God.' So it was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went to the Sacred Mosque where the chiefs of Quraysh were, and he stood over their heads and recited it to them, and they despaired."

Perhaps their calling "O" (*ya ayyuha*) was for the sake of emphasis in seeking their attention, lest anything of what is addressed to them escape them. And (the use of) "the disbelievers" (*al-kafirun*) rather than "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) is because disbelief was their ancient religion and did not newly arise for them; or because the address is to those whose continuance in disbelief is known, so it is as if it were necessary for them; or for hastening to mention what is to be said to them, because of the great concern for it. And it is with this (designation) and not "the polytheists," although they were idol-worshippers, and the more common expression for them is this, because what is mentioned is more wounding to them, and so it is more effective in cutting off their empty hopes.

It has been said: this is to indicate that disbelief is all one religion (community). It is not far-fetched that in this indication there is also a wounding to them. And in his, peace be upon him, calling them by this in their assembly and the place where they spread their hands, there is evidence of his, peace be upon him, lack of concern for them; for the meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad," and the intended meaning is the reality of the command, contrary to the author of *al-Ta'wilat*, who (took it as) "for the disbelievers": ﴿O you disbelievers﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 109, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾ ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾. It appears that there is repetition in it for the sake of emphasis (ta'kid). Thus the third sentence, the negated one, according to what is in al-Bahr, is an emphasis of the first, in a more eloquent manner, because of the emphatic nominal form (ismiyyah, nominal sentence). The fourth is an emphasis of the second. This is the view chosen by al-Tibi, and al-Farra' went in that direction and said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and it is their custom to repeat speech for emphasis and clarification. So the respondent says: "Yes, yes" (bala bala), and the one who refuses says: "No, no" (la la). On this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ ﴿Again, no! You will come to know﴾. He also recited his saying:

Many a favour they have done me, which they bestowed upon me and made obligatory,

and his saying:

The crow called out at dawn about Layla's separation: "How much, how much," and with Layla's parting it keeps calling.

And his saying:

Why did you not ask the assemblies of Kin-dah on the day they turned back, "Where, where are we?"

This is common in verse and in prose. The benefit of emphasis here is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers and to confirm that they will remain in disbelief forever.

It has been objected that the emphasis of sentences with a conjunction is only possible with thumma (then), and that whoever said this seems to have analogised waw (and) to thumma. The apparent meaning is that whoever holds the view of emphasis made the fourth sentence coordinated with the third, and made the whole group coordinated with the group of the first two sentences. So there are two coordinated groups, the second of which emphasises the first. Because the second differs from the first in its implication of continuity, it is joined to it with waw, so what was mentioned does not apply. This includes the meaning of the first part of the second emphasising the first part of the first, and the second part of the second emphasising the second part of the first. Otherwise, the apparent meaning in al-Bahr is something that is hardly permissible, as is not hidden.

What the majority hold is that there is no repetition in it, but they differed. Al-Zamakhshari said: (﴿I do not worship﴾) is intended to negate worship in the future, because la (not) only enters upon a present-tense verb with future meaning, just as ma (not) only enters upon a present-tense verb with present meaning. The meaning is: I will not do in the future what you ask of me, namely worshipping your gods; nor will you do in it what I ask of you, namely worshipping my God. And I have never been a worshipper in the past of what you worshipped, nor have you worshipped at the time when I am devoted to worship. Apparently he took into account in the last sentence the continuity of the negation, and he understood the present tense there to convey continuity and depiction. In the second, the negation encompasses past times.

Al-Tibi said: he made the two latter sentences refer to the first two as future, and the last two as past. It was objected to him that the two restrictions he mentioned in la and ma are not correct, even though the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words suggests them.

Al-Khafaji said: what has been mentioned is generally the case, or it is restricted to the absence of an indicator that contradicts it, or it is universal, and there is no barrier to figurative usage and interpreting it otherwise for a reason, such as avoiding repetition here. Even if it is said that the strangeness is established on the view that it is a condition in narration for the one who worships in the first, and that the loss of it is harmless in the second, because the accusative with it is for harmony (mashakalah, harmony of wording). It was also said: the first two indicate the future, as already mentioned, and the last two indicate the present. This was chosen by Abu Hayyan, that is: I am not, at present, a worshipper of your objects of worship, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my object of worship.

It was said the reverse, and on this is the speech of al-Zajjaj and Muhyi al-Sunnah. It was said: the first two refer to the past and the last two to the future. This was related by Ibn Kathir from the narration of al-Bukhari and others. It is also reported from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah that what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is negation of the act, because it is a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah). And by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ is negation of his, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, acceptance of that altogether, because negation with a nominal sentence is stronger, so it is as if he negated the act. His, peace be upon him, being capable of that and its meaning being negation of occurrence and negation of its legal possibility. It has been disputed whether a nominal sentence conveys negation of acceptance. It is not far-fetched to say that the meaning of a verbal sentence is negation of the act at a specific time, while the meaning of a nominal sentence is negation of entry under this concept absolutely, without reference to time, as if it were said: I am one of those to whom this concept does not apply at all, and you are among those to whom that concept does not apply. So reflect.

[p. 252]

It was also said: the first two are for negating the consideration which the disbelievers mentioned, and the last two are for general negation. That is: I do not worship what you worship, hoping that you will worship God exalted, nor will you worship, hoping that I will worship your idol. Then it was said: nor am I a worshipper of your idol for any purpose and in any way, and likewise you do not worship God exalted for any purpose. The choice of ma in ﴿what I worship﴾ was said to be over all the preceding views, in contrast to man (who), because the intended meaning is the attribute, as if it were said: what I worship is the Being of great majesty whose greatness cannot be measured. It is also permissible to say: since ma was first applied to idols, and this is application in its proper place, it was applied to the God who is truly worshipped by way of mashakalah. As for one who says that ma may apply to what is rational, and this is attributed to Sibawayh, it does not need what has been mentioned. Abu Muslim said: ma in the first two is in the sense of "that which" (alladhi) as an object, and the intended meaning is the worshipped: that is, I do not worship the idols, and you do not worship God exalted. In the last two, ma is verbal-noun (masdariyyah), that is: nor am I a worshipper with the same worship as yours, which is based on doubt. And if you wish, you may say: based on polytheism, which removes it from being true worship. Nor will you be worshippers with the same worship as mine, which is based on certainty. And if you wish, you may say: based on monotheism and sincerity. On this view too, there is no repetition.

Some eminent scholars said in this context: the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ are either both negation of the present, or both negation of the future, or one of them is for the present and the other for the future. In all these cases, ma is either verbal-noun in both places, or relative (mawsulah) or descriptive (mawsufah) in both, or verbal-noun in one and relative or descriptive in the other. These are six possibilities arising from multiplying three by two. No attention was paid to dividing the situation of difference into the distinction between the first and the second, nor to the distinction between the relative and the descriptive, so that the divisions would not multiply, because the forms of difference are equal in avoiding repetition, and the meaning of the relative and the descriptive are close, so one of them suffices. The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places. It is known that there is no repetition in the form of difference, whether it is in terms of present and future, or in terms of ma being relative or descriptive in one and verbal-noun in the other. The negation of their worship, in the present or future, of what he worshipped, peace be upon him, is based on not counting their worship of God as valid, because of the shirk that nullifies it and turns it into scattered dust, as it has been said:

If your friend makes peace with the one you oppose, he has become your enemy, and speech is cut off.

From here, one of the eminent scholars said, in removing the verse from repetition: It may be that what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is negation of worship of idols, and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ is negation of worship of God exalted, without addressing anything else. And since there was a likelihood that they would say, out of heedlessness of the intended meaning or the like: How is it proper for you to negate from yourself the worship of what we worship, and from us the worship of what you worship, when we too worship God exalted? At most, we worship another alongside Him. He followed this with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, and so on, to indicate that they did not truly worship God, but worshipped something they claimed was God, while God, mighty and majestic, is beyond that. That is: nor am I, at any time, a worshipper of the God you have worshipped, because you worshipped something you imagined, and this, under the title of what you imagined, is not the God I worship. Nor will you, at any time, be worshippers of what I am devoted to worshipping, because I only worship the God characterised by the attributes for which proof has been established that they are the attributes of God.

[The inner (nafs amri) reading]

From this a different aspect may be known, apart from what preceded, for the expression "the disbelievers" rather than "the polytheists". It seems that the first two sentences were not given with this meaning, and it is sufficient with them in place of the last two, because they are more fitting to their answer, and this style is more painful to them. So do not overlook it.

Some people chose that ma in the first two sentences is relative, an object of what precedes it, and what is meant by it first is their gods, and second is his God, peace be upon him. The intended meaning is negation of worship, considering it together with what it is connected to of the object. Indeed, the object is the aim and focus of attention, as the placement of the two sentences in the answer requires. He takes the future into account, observing the more common usage of la when it enters upon a present-tense verb, and this is also more fitting to the answer. It is complete in their case. So it is as if it were said: I will not worship in the future what you worship in the present of the gods, that is: I will not bring that about according to what you ask of me and call me to. Nor will you worship in the future what I worship in the present. And as for the last two being verbal-noun, with what follows them construed as a verbal noun that is placed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of what precedes, as Abu Muslim did, so that the speech includes an indication of explaining the state of worship in itself, without regard to its connection with the object, although in reality it is not free of it, following the indication of explaining its state along with considering its connection with the object. The intended meaning is continuity of negation in both, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. In this there is more painful effect than there is in limiting it to what the answer is complete with. So it is as if it were said: nor am I, continuously, a worshipper with worship like your worship, with which you have wasted your lives, because my worship is commanded, and your worship is forbidden. Nor will you, continuously, be worshippers with worship like my worship, which I am continuously engaged in, because you are those whom God exalted has forsaken, and He has sealed their hearts. And I am the beloved, sent with the truth. So you remain in a worship that is forbidden, and I remain in a worship that is commanded. You may also consider the difference between the two forms of worship in another way. The consideration of continuity in "what I worship" is indicated by the shift away from "what I have worshipped", which is what "what you have worshipped" before it requires, and the shift in the second to that is because his, peace be upon him, forms of worship were not yet complete; rather, new forms continued to be added to them. So he used what conveys renewing continuity, to indicate the truth of all that he, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, brings of that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he did not say "what I have worshipped" as it was said "what you have worshipped", because they used to worship idols before the mission (ba'th), and he, peace be upon him, did not worship God exalted at that time. This was criticised, since there is a problem with it, because it is established that he, peace be upon him, used to devote himself to worship in the cave of Hira before the prophethood.

Abu al-Wafa' attributed to Ibn 'Aqil the view that the Prophet (ﷺ) was following a religious practice before his mission that is authentically reported to have come from the law (shari'a) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). After the mission, Ibn al-Jawzi said in *Kitab al-Wafa'*: there are two reports from Imam Ahmad. The first is that he was bound to worship according to what was authentically established from the laws of earlier prophets, through revelation, and not from their own transmission, their narrations, or their corrupted books. Abu al-Hasan al-Tamimi chose this view, and it is the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa. The second is that he was bound only to what was revealed to him of his own law. This is the view of the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ariyya. The followers of al-Shafi'i have two opinions, like the two reports. Those who hold that the Prophet (peace be upon him) was bound to the law of those before him disagree about the specifics. Some say he was bound to the law of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and this is the view of the followers of al-Shafi'i. Others say he was bound to the law of Musa (peace be upon him), except what was abrogated in our law. The apparent meaning of Ahmad's words is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was bound to everything that is authentically established as a law of a prophet before him, as long as its abrogation has not been established, based on the saying of God Most High: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: the Arabs continued to hold remnants of the religion of Isma'il (peace be upon him), such as the pilgrimage, circumcision, the pronouncement of triple divorce, blood-money, the ritual bath after sexual impurity, and the prohibition of marrying those forbidden by kinship or by marriage. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was upon what they held of belief in God Most High and acting in accordance with their laws. End of quotation.

The Mu'tazila did not permit this, claiming that it involves a corruption, namely that it would make people averse. Yes, among their principles is the obligation of rational worship through reflection on the signs of God Most High and the proofs of His oneness, glorified is He, and of knowing Him, mighty and majestic is He. It is not possible for the Prophet (ﷺ) to neglect this.

In *al-Kashf*: worship (ʿibada) is sometimes applied to acts of the limbs performed as drawing near to God. Thus faith, intention, and sincerity are conditions. From this is the saying: "One jurist is more formidable to Satan than a thousand worshippers."

There is disagreement over whether the Prophet (peace be upon him) was bound by this meaning before his prophethood, through a law or not. The inclination of Imam Fakhr al-Din, a group of Shafi'is, and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and his followers is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not bound. They answered regarding circumambulation (tawaf), seclusion for worship (tahannuth), and other noble practices, that they are not forbidden without a law, so it cannot be said that whoever performs them must have been bound. Rather, they arise from habitual customs and innate noble dispositions, without regard to drawing near to God. Al-Zamakhshari chose this view and built his commentary upon it. It has become clear that he did not contradict his principle regarding the obligation of rational worship through reflection on the signs and the proofs of oneness and knowledge. Then he said: the apparent meaning is to take "what I worship" (ma a'bud) as indicating continuity, and the depiction is that they did not deny what the Prophet (ﷺ) did in the past, whether it was worship or not. Rather, they used to honor him and call him "the Trustworthy" (al-Amin). The denial was only of what he did after prophethood. Therefore it was said secondly: ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾, for if it had been said "what I have worshipped," it would not have fit the context. In this there is a point that what they imagined of his agreement with them before prophethood was not correct; rather, that was only because he (peace be upon him) had not yet been commanded to call to the faith. End of quotation. So reflect on it. Some have claimed that the variation of expressions in this surah is due to the variation of the states of the two groups, but this is not correct. As for imposing what has been mentioned on these addressees, if the meaning is continuity upon disbelief in faith, there is a discussion mentioned in the books of legal theory. If you want it, return to it. It will come, God willing, in the commentary on Surat Tabbat, with some allusion to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 109, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾ ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾. It appears that there is repetition in it for the sake of emphasis (ta'kid). Thus the third sentence, the negated one, according to what is in al-Bahr, is an emphasis of the first, in a more eloquent manner, because of the emphatic nominal form (ismiyyah, nominal sentence). The fourth is an emphasis of the second. This is the view chosen by al-Tibi, and al-Farra' went in that direction and said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and it is their custom to repeat speech for emphasis and clarification. So the respondent says: "Yes, yes" (bala bala), and the one who refuses says: "No, no" (la la). On this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ ﴿Again, no! You will come to know﴾. He also recited his saying:

Many a favour they have done me, which they bestowed upon me and made obligatory,

and his saying:

The crow called out at dawn about Layla's separation: "How much, how much," and with Layla's parting it keeps calling.

And his saying:

Why did you not ask the assemblies of Kin-dah on the day they turned back, "Where, where are we?"

This is common in verse and in prose. The benefit of emphasis here is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers and to confirm that they will remain in disbelief forever.

It has been objected that the emphasis of sentences with a conjunction is only possible with thumma (then), and that whoever said this seems to have analogised waw (and) to thumma. The apparent meaning is that whoever holds the view of emphasis made the fourth sentence coordinated with the third, and made the whole group coordinated with the group of the first two sentences. So there are two coordinated groups, the second of which emphasises the first. Because the second differs from the first in its implication of continuity, it is joined to it with waw, so what was mentioned does not apply. This includes the meaning of the first part of the second emphasising the first part of the first, and the second part of the second emphasising the second part of the first. Otherwise, the apparent meaning in al-Bahr is something that is hardly permissible, as is not hidden.

What the majority hold is that there is no repetition in it, but they differed. Al-Zamakhshari said: (﴿I do not worship﴾) is intended to negate worship in the future, because la (not) only enters upon a present-tense verb with future meaning, just as ma (not) only enters upon a present-tense verb with present meaning. The meaning is: I will not do in the future what you ask of me, namely worshipping your gods; nor will you do in it what I ask of you, namely worshipping my God. And I have never been a worshipper in the past of what you worshipped, nor have you worshipped at the time when I am devoted to worship. Apparently he took into account in the last sentence the continuity of the negation, and he understood the present tense there to convey continuity and depiction. In the second, the negation encompasses past times.

Al-Tibi said: he made the two latter sentences refer to the first two as future, and the last two as past. It was objected to him that the two restrictions he mentioned in la and ma are not correct, even though the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words suggests them.

Al-Khafaji said: what has been mentioned is generally the case, or it is restricted to the absence of an indicator that contradicts it, or it is universal, and there is no barrier to figurative usage and interpreting it otherwise for a reason, such as avoiding repetition here. Even if it is said that the strangeness is established on the view that it is a condition in narration for the one who worships in the first, and that the loss of it is harmless in the second, because the accusative with it is for harmony (mashakalah, harmony of wording). It was also said: the first two indicate the future, as already mentioned, and the last two indicate the present. This was chosen by Abu Hayyan, that is: I am not, at present, a worshipper of your objects of worship, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my object of worship.

It was said the reverse, and on this is the speech of al-Zajjaj and Muhyi al-Sunnah. It was said: the first two refer to the past and the last two to the future. This was related by Ibn Kathir from the narration of al-Bukhari and others. It is also reported from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah that what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is negation of the act, because it is a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah). And by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ is negation of his, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, acceptance of that altogether, because negation with a nominal sentence is stronger, so it is as if he negated the act. His, peace be upon him, being capable of that and its meaning being negation of occurrence and negation of its legal possibility. It has been disputed whether a nominal sentence conveys negation of acceptance. It is not far-fetched to say that the meaning of a verbal sentence is negation of the act at a specific time, while the meaning of a nominal sentence is negation of entry under this concept absolutely, without reference to time, as if it were said: I am one of those to whom this concept does not apply at all, and you are among those to whom that concept does not apply. So reflect.

[p. 252]

It was also said: the first two are for negating the consideration which the disbelievers mentioned, and the last two are for general negation. That is: I do not worship what you worship, hoping that you will worship God exalted, nor will you worship, hoping that I will worship your idol. Then it was said: nor am I a worshipper of your idol for any purpose and in any way, and likewise you do not worship God exalted for any purpose. The choice of ma in ﴿what I worship﴾ was said to be over all the preceding views, in contrast to man (who), because the intended meaning is the attribute, as if it were said: what I worship is the Being of great majesty whose greatness cannot be measured. It is also permissible to say: since ma was first applied to idols, and this is application in its proper place, it was applied to the God who is truly worshipped by way of mashakalah. As for one who says that ma may apply to what is rational, and this is attributed to Sibawayh, it does not need what has been mentioned. Abu Muslim said: ma in the first two is in the sense of "that which" (alladhi) as an object, and the intended meaning is the worshipped: that is, I do not worship the idols, and you do not worship God exalted. In the last two, ma is verbal-noun (masdariyyah), that is: nor am I a worshipper with the same worship as yours, which is based on doubt. And if you wish, you may say: based on polytheism, which removes it from being true worship. Nor will you be worshippers with the same worship as mine, which is based on certainty. And if you wish, you may say: based on monotheism and sincerity. On this view too, there is no repetition.

Some eminent scholars said in this context: the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ are either both negation of the present, or both negation of the future, or one of them is for the present and the other for the future. In all these cases, ma is either verbal-noun in both places, or relative (mawsulah) or descriptive (mawsufah) in both, or verbal-noun in one and relative or descriptive in the other. These are six possibilities arising from multiplying three by two. No attention was paid to dividing the situation of difference into the distinction between the first and the second, nor to the distinction between the relative and the descriptive, so that the divisions would not multiply, because the forms of difference are equal in avoiding repetition, and the meaning of the relative and the descriptive are close, so one of them suffices. The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places. It is known that there is no repetition in the form of difference, whether it is in terms of present and future, or in terms of ma being relative or descriptive in one and verbal-noun in the other. The negation of their worship, in the present or future, of what he worshipped, peace be upon him, is based on not counting their worship of God as valid, because of the shirk that nullifies it and turns it into scattered dust, as it has been said:

If your friend makes peace with the one you oppose, he has become your enemy, and speech is cut off.

From here, one of the eminent scholars said, in removing the verse from repetition: It may be that what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is negation of worship of idols, and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ is negation of worship of God exalted, without addressing anything else. And since there was a likelihood that they would say, out of heedlessness of the intended meaning or the like: How is it proper for you to negate from yourself the worship of what we worship, and from us the worship of what you worship, when we too worship God exalted? At most, we worship another alongside Him. He followed this with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, and so on, to indicate that they did not truly worship God, but worshipped something they claimed was God, while God, mighty and majestic, is beyond that. That is: nor am I, at any time, a worshipper of the God you have worshipped, because you worshipped something you imagined, and this, under the title of what you imagined, is not the God I worship. Nor will you, at any time, be worshippers of what I am devoted to worshipping, because I only worship the God characterised by the attributes for which proof has been established that they are the attributes of God.

[The inner (nafs amri) reading]

From this a different aspect may be known, apart from what preceded, for the expression "the disbelievers" rather than "the polytheists". It seems that the first two sentences were not given with this meaning, and it is sufficient with them in place of the last two, because they are more fitting to their answer, and this style is more painful to them. So do not overlook it.

Some people chose that ma in the first two sentences is relative, an object of what precedes it, and what is meant by it first is their gods, and second is his God, peace be upon him. The intended meaning is negation of worship, considering it together with what it is connected to of the object. Indeed, the object is the aim and focus of attention, as the placement of the two sentences in the answer requires. He takes the future into account, observing the more common usage of la when it enters upon a present-tense verb, and this is also more fitting to the answer. It is complete in their case. So it is as if it were said: I will not worship in the future what you worship in the present of the gods, that is: I will not bring that about according to what you ask of me and call me to. Nor will you worship in the future what I worship in the present. And as for the last two being verbal-noun, with what follows them construed as a verbal noun that is placed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of what precedes, as Abu Muslim did, so that the speech includes an indication of explaining the state of worship in itself, without regard to its connection with the object, although in reality it is not free of it, following the indication of explaining its state along with considering its connection with the object. The intended meaning is continuity of negation in both, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. In this there is more painful effect than there is in limiting it to what the answer is complete with. So it is as if it were said: nor am I, continuously, a worshipper with worship like your worship, with which you have wasted your lives, because my worship is commanded, and your worship is forbidden. Nor will you, continuously, be worshippers with worship like my worship, which I am continuously engaged in, because you are those whom God exalted has forsaken, and He has sealed their hearts. And I am the beloved, sent with the truth. So you remain in a worship that is forbidden, and I remain in a worship that is commanded. You may also consider the difference between the two forms of worship in another way. The consideration of continuity in "what I worship" is indicated by the shift away from "what I have worshipped", which is what "what you have worshipped" before it requires, and the shift in the second to that is because his, peace be upon him, forms of worship were not yet complete; rather, new forms continued to be added to them. So he used what conveys renewing continuity, to indicate the truth of all that he, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, brings of that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he did not say "what I have worshipped" as it was said "what you have worshipped", because they used to worship idols before the mission (ba'th), and he, peace be upon him, did not worship God exalted at that time. This was criticised, since there is a problem with it, because it is established that he, peace be upon him, used to devote himself to worship in the cave of Hira before the prophethood.

Abu al-Wafa' attributed to Ibn 'Aqil the view that the Prophet (ﷺ) was following a religious practice before his mission that is authentically reported to have come from the law (shari'a) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). After the mission, Ibn al-Jawzi said in *Kitab al-Wafa'*: there are two reports from Imam Ahmad. The first is that he was bound to worship according to what was authentically established from the laws of earlier prophets, through revelation, and not from their own transmission, their narrations, or their corrupted books. Abu al-Hasan al-Tamimi chose this view, and it is the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa. The second is that he was bound only to what was revealed to him of his own law. This is the view of the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ariyya. The followers of al-Shafi'i have two opinions, like the two reports. Those who hold that the Prophet (peace be upon him) was bound to the law of those before him disagree about the specifics. Some say he was bound to the law of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and this is the view of the followers of al-Shafi'i. Others say he was bound to the law of Musa (peace be upon him), except what was abrogated in our law. The apparent meaning of Ahmad's words is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was bound to everything that is authentically established as a law of a prophet before him, as long as its abrogation has not been established, based on the saying of God Most High: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: the Arabs continued to hold remnants of the religion of Isma'il (peace be upon him), such as the pilgrimage, circumcision, the pronouncement of triple divorce, blood-money, the ritual bath after sexual impurity, and the prohibition of marrying those forbidden by kinship or by marriage. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was upon what they held of belief in God Most High and acting in accordance with their laws. End of quotation.

The Mu'tazila did not permit this, claiming that it involves a corruption, namely that it would make people averse. Yes, among their principles is the obligation of rational worship through reflection on the signs of God Most High and the proofs of His oneness, glorified is He, and of knowing Him, mighty and majestic is He. It is not possible for the Prophet (ﷺ) to neglect this.

In *al-Kashf*: worship (ʿibada) is sometimes applied to acts of the limbs performed as drawing near to God. Thus faith, intention, and sincerity are conditions. From this is the saying: "One jurist is more formidable to Satan than a thousand worshippers."

There is disagreement over whether the Prophet (peace be upon him) was bound by this meaning before his prophethood, through a law or not. The inclination of Imam Fakhr al-Din, a group of Shafi'is, and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and his followers is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not bound. They answered regarding circumambulation (tawaf), seclusion for worship (tahannuth), and other noble practices, that they are not forbidden without a law, so it cannot be said that whoever performs them must have been bound. Rather, they arise from habitual customs and innate noble dispositions, without regard to drawing near to God. Al-Zamakhshari chose this view and built his commentary upon it. It has become clear that he did not contradict his principle regarding the obligation of rational worship through reflection on the signs and the proofs of oneness and knowledge. Then he said: the apparent meaning is to take "what I worship" (ma a'bud) as indicating continuity, and the depiction is that they did not deny what the Prophet (ﷺ) did in the past, whether it was worship or not. Rather, they used to honor him and call him "the Trustworthy" (al-Amin). The denial was only of what he did after prophethood. Therefore it was said secondly: ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾, for if it had been said "what I have worshipped," it would not have fit the context. In this there is a point that what they imagined of his agreement with them before prophethood was not correct; rather, that was only because he (peace be upon him) had not yet been commanded to call to the faith. End of quotation. So reflect on it. Some have claimed that the variation of expressions in this surah is due to the variation of the states of the two groups, but this is not correct. As for imposing what has been mentioned on these addressees, if the meaning is continuity upon disbelief in faith, there is a discussion mentioned in the books of legal theory. If you want it, return to it. It will come, God willing, in the commentary on Surat Tabbat, with some allusion to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 109, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is, according to most scholars, a confirmation (taqrir) of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, just as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and for me is my religion﴾ is, in their view, a confirmation of His saying: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾. The meaning is: your religion, which is polytheism (al-ishrak), is restricted to being yours and does not extend beyond you to being attained as you hope for it. So do not hang your empty wishes upon it, for that is among the impossibilities. And my religion, which is monotheism (al-tawhid), is restricted to being mine and does not extend beyond me to being yours either, because God, Exalted is He, has sealed your hearts on account of your poor predisposition (su' isti'dadikum), or because you have tied it to the impossibility that is my worshipping your gods or my touching (istilam) them, or because what you promise (wa'adtumuh) is itself polytheism. And since their intention was the partnership of the two groups in both acts of worship, the restriction (qasr) derived from placing the predicate first (taqdim al-musnad) was necessarily a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad).

It has also been permitted that this be a confirmation of His saying: ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾. On what has been mentioned, the verse is decisive (muhkamah), not abrogated (ghayr mansukhah), as is not hidden. Or the intended meaning is abandonment (al-mutaraka), in the sense: I am a prophet sent to you to call you to the truth and salvation; so if you do not accept from me and do not follow me, then leave me to my own (da'uni kafafan), and do not call me to polytheism. On this view, as more than one scholar said, it is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The word din has been interpreted as reckoning (hisab), i.e., for you is your reckoning and for me is my reckoning; no effect of one party's deed on the other returns to either of us. It has also been interpreted as recompense (jaza'), i.e., for you is your recompense and for me is my recompense. It has been said: the statement on both interpretations is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it was said: "What will happen if we remain upon the worship of our gods, and if I remain upon the worship of your God?" So it was said: "(For you) etc." The meaning is: evil will be theirs, and good will be his, upon him be prayer and peace. However, the lam in "lakum" was used for the sake of correspondence (li-l-mushakalah), and on this view there is also no abrogation. It is possible that the intended meaning is other than that, by which the verse would be abrogated, and perhaps this is not hidden.

The word din may also be interpreted as state (al-hal), as it is one of its meanings according to what al-Qali mentioned in his Amali and others; i.e., for you is your state fitting for you, which your poor predisposition requires, and for me is my state fitting for me, which my good predisposition requires. The sentence on this interpretation is like a justification (ta'lil) for what the preceding statement contained, so there is no abrogation. The preferable course is to interpret it in a way on which it is not abrogated, because abrogation (naskh) is contrary to the apparent meaning, so it is not resorted to except in necessity. Imam al-Razi has several interpretations of it, some of which are not free from scrutiny.

He, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that it has become customary for people to invoke this verse when parting ways (al-mutaraka); and this is not permissible, because the Qur'an was not sent down to be invoked in that manner, but to be guided by. There is in this a leaning toward closing the door of iqtibas (applying Qur'anic phrases in other contexts), whereas the correct view is its permissibility; for it occurred in the speech of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, and in the speech of many of the Companions, the imams, and the Successors. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti has a comprehensive and sufficient treatise on removing confusion regarding the permissibility of iqtibas, and what has been cited as evidence against it is too evident to need pointing out its weakness. Sallam and Ya'qub read "dini" with a ya' both in continuation and in pause, while the seven readers omitted it. And God, Exalted is He, knows best.
